chunks: As for what Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated, from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Ḥammād ibn ʿUthmān, from al-Ḥalabī, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said:

Regarding stale water: you may perform wudu (ablution) from it unless you find other water besides it. This does not contradict the first two reports, because the correct understanding in this report is when the water has changed by itself or by being adjacent to a pure object, for the prohibited use is only when it has changed due to impurity affecting it. According to this understanding, there is no contradiction between the reports.

key_terms.النَّجَاسَةِ: ritual impurity that renders the water unusable
key_terms.الْأَخْبَارِ: the reports or hadith being reconciled
key_terms.الْمَاءِ الْآجِنِ: stale or altered water that has changed without impurity
key_terms.الْمَحْظُورَ: that which is prohibited to use
key_terms.تَغَيَّرَ: it changed in one of its qualities
key_terms.جِسْمٍ طَاهِرٍ: a pure object whose proximity may affect the water

ai.seo_question: Can wudu (ablution) be performed with stale or altered water if its color, taste, or smell has changed?
ai.summary: This text explains the legal ruling on using stale or altered water for wudu (ablution). It reconciles apparently conflicting reports by distinguishing between water changed by natural causes or a pure neighboring object, which remains usable, and water changed by najasah, which is prohibited.
